newsitem.title: CHILE: Argentine, Chilean leaders urge treaty passage.
newsitem.headline: Argentine, Chilean leaders urge treaty passage.

text.p: The presidents of Chile and Argentina made a final pitch to their parliaments on Tuesday to ratify a 1991 border treaty, saying the future of the two countries' ambitious cooperation plans was at stake.

Argentina's Carlos Menem and Chilean Eduardo Frei both urged early passage of the treaty setting the border over a vast Patagonian glacier known in Chile as the Ice Fields. The treaty has gone nowhere in either Congress and was likely to face serious opposition, especially in Chile, when it comes up for debate, possibly this month.

The two foreign ministers signed a "protocol" clarifying a few points in the original treaty such as use of water rights in the area and reaffirming that Mount Fitz Roy lies on the border and not on the Argentine side. Suspicious Chilean legislators had charged that the treaty put the jagged peak squarely in Argentina.
The treaty applies to a remote, roadless area about 1,100 miles (1,700 km) south of Santiago where year-round snow and ice stretch from the Andes Mountains to the Pacific coast.

Officials of both countries said the real reason for Menem's four-hour visit to Chile was to give a political push to the treaty, aimed at settling a stubborn point of friction as both countries move toward closer economic ties.
"God willing, (the treaty) will be passed by the end of the year," Menem told reporters upon arrival in Santiago.

"We have left behind, once and for all, the moments of fear and mistrust that used to separate us ... Congressmen, you have the unique opportunity to culminate this work of peace," Frei said at the signing ceremony.

But nationalistic Chilean legislators were unconvinced. "What Frei has done is surrender to Menem a piece of our sovereignty. Chile is in serious danger because this could happen again with any other bordering country," deputy Ivan Moreira of the rightist Independent Democratic Union said.

Frei's centre-left government should have no trouble getting the treaty through the Chamber of Deputies, where it has a majority. Prospects are less clear in the Senate, where rightist parties and military-appointed senators hold a narrow majority.
